welcome.title: Start here
welcome.description: Kubernetes looks scary because people show you everything at once. We won't. You'll learn one idea at a time, each one fixing a real problem, and you'll…
welcome.html:
Kubernetes looks scary because people show you everything at once. We won't. You'll learn one idea at a time, each one fixing a real problem, and you'll play with a tiny fake cluster right here on the page.

Begin here. Nothing to install today. Follow Guided learning from top to bottom. Read one lesson, try its practice, answer its questions, then choose Next. Stop whenever you like; your place is saved.

First tiny goal: explain “Kubernetes keeps the number of app copies I asked for.” You do not need to memorize commands. In Stages 1–4, code blocks are examples to read. Stage 5 tells you when to open a real terminal.

Six words to know before you begin
  • App: a program that does a job, such as serving a website.
  • Server: a computer that runs an app and answers requests.
  • Request: a message asking the app to do something, such as show a page.
  • Terminal: a window where you type commands for your computer.
  • kubectl: the command-line tool you use to ask Kubernetes to show or change something.
  • K8s: a short name for Kubernetes. The 8 stands for the eight letters between K and s.

Your path, with a finish line for each stage

1 · Understand the pieces · lessons 1–5Start with “Why does Kubernetes exist?” Finish when you can explain an image, a container, a node, a Pod, and the desired-state loop in your own words.
2 · Run and reach an app · lessons 6–9Practice replacing a deleted pod, recovering from a lost machine, and sending requests through a Service. Finish when you can trace browser → entry point → Service → ready Pod.
3 · Give the app what it needs · lessons 10–12Learn settings, passwords, disks, health checks, and capacity. Finish when you can fix a waiting pod and explain why stored data needs a volume and a backup.
4 · Update and fix it · lessons 13–16Ship a good version, recover from a broken one, solve the debugging cases, and learn permissions. Finish when you can choose the first command to investigate a failure.
5 · Do it for real · lessons 17–20Build the laptop cluster first. Repeat its deploy, break, and undo exercises without looking. Then build the k3s home lab, practice a restore, and complete the Graduation checklist.

Pace: one or two lessons per sitting is enough. Repeat a simulation until you can predict what will happen before clicking. A wrong answer is a chance to try again.

Explore the cluster is the optional detailed lab. Save it until after Stage 2, or use it when you want to inspect a specific concept. You can finish the guided path without reading all 41 detailed lessons.

How every lesson works

🎬 a problem→💡 one idea that fixes it→🎮 play with it→✅ 2–4 quick questions→📌 what to remember

Each lesson takes about 5–10 minutes. Your progress is saved in this browser. Some games have a ⭐ challenge. Collect them all.

Our example app for the whole course: 🍕 Pizza Express, a small web app in a container. We'll take it from “runs on my laptop” to “runs on a cluster that fixes itself”.

By the end you'll have built a 3-machine cluster, deployed an app, updated it, broken it, fixed it, and learned how to keep it running. Ready?

why.title: Why does Kubernetes exist?
why.description: Your 🍕 app runs in a container on one server. Life is good… until: Friday night, traffic triples → everything gets slow. 2am, the app crashes → nobody…
why.html:
The problem
Your 🍕 app runs in a container on one server. Life is good… until:
  • Friday night, traffic triples → everything gets slow.
  • 2am, the app crashes → nobody restarts it until you wake up.
  • The server's disk dies → the app is gone.
  • You ship a new version → you stop the old one, start the new one, and customers see errors in between.
So you start writing scripts to fix all this… congratulations, you're building Kubernetes. Badly. 😅
The big idea
Kubernetes is a robot operator. You don't tell it what to do. You tell it what you want, like “3 copies of pizza:v1, always”, and it works 24/7 to make reality match your wish.
Think of it like…
A thermostat 🌡️. You set 22°C. You don't switch the heater on and off yourself. If someone opens a window, the thermostat notices and fixes it.
📝 You write a wish
“3 copies”→👀 K8s checks reality
“only 2 running”→🔧 K8s fixes the gap
starts 1 more→🔁 repeat forever

This loop is called reconciliation, and honestly it's 80% of Kubernetes. Almost every other feature just gives that loop one more thing to keep correct.

Do I even need it?

For one tiny app, a single server or a hosting platform is simpler. Kubernetes is worth it when you have several services, need updates with no downtime, want apps to restart themselves and to scale. It's also the industry standard, so learning it pays off.

Remember
  • You describe the desired state. Kubernetes makes the actual state match.
  • The compare-and-fix loop runs forever. It's at the heart of everything.

quiz.q: You told Kubernetes “run 3 copies”. One copy crashes at 2am. What happens?
options: Nothing until you wake up and restart it
Kubernetes notices 2 ≠ 3 and starts a new copy
quiz.why: That's the loop: wanted 3, have 2, so start one. You keep sleeping.

quiz.q: How do you talk to Kubernetes?
options: Give it step-by-step instructions: start this, then that
Describe the end result you want and let it work out the steps
Log into each server and run docker commands
quiz.why: This is called declarative: you describe where you want to end up, not how to get there.

containers.title: Containers in 2 minutes
containers.description: “It works on my machine!” is the oldest excuse in software. Your app needs Python 3.12 and certain libraries, and the server has something else installed.…
containers.html:
The problem
“It works on my machine!” is the oldest excuse in software. Your app needs Python 3.12 and certain libraries, and the server has something else installed.
The big idea
An image is a sealed package: your app plus everything it needs, frozen. A container is that image running. One image can run as many containers as you want.
Think of it like…
An image is a laminated recipe card. A container is a dish cooked from it. You can cook 10 dishes from one card.

Images live in a registry (Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry, …) with a name and a tag, like nginx:1.27. Kubernetes downloads (“pulls”) images from there. That's all you need to know about containers for this course.

📄 A Dockerfile for our pizza app (no need to write one yet)
FROM python:3.12-slim
COPY . /app
RUN pip install -r /app/requirements.txt
CMD ["python", "/app/server.py"]
docker build -t myname/pizza:v1 .  # use your registry username
docker push myname/pizza:v1     # upload it to a registry so a cluster can pull it
Remember
  • Image = frozen package. Container = a running copy of it.
  • Kubernetes runs containers. It does not build them.

quiz.q: What's the difference between an image and a container?
options: Image = the packaged app (frozen); container = a running copy of it
Container = the package; image = a screenshot of it
quiz.why: One image can run as many containers as you want.

quiz.q: Where does Kubernetes get your image from?
options: It builds it from your source code
You copy it to each server on a USB stick
quiz.why: You build the image and push it. Kubernetes pulls it.

cluster.title: The cluster: a brain and some muscles
cluster.description: One server isn't enough: it can die, and it can only do so much. So you get 3 machines. Now who decides which app runs where? Who notices when a machine…
cluster.html:
The problem
One server isn't enough: it can die, and it can only do so much. So you get 3 machines. Now who decides which app runs where? Who notices when a machine dies?
The big idea
A cluster is a group of machines called nodes. Some of them form the control plane (the brain 🧠). The rest are worker nodes (the muscles 💪) that actually run your containers.
Think of it like…
A restaurant 🍽️. The office (control plane) takes orders and decides who cooks what. The kitchen stations (worker nodes) do the cooking.

Click each part to see what it does:

🧠 Control plane
🚪 API server“The order counter.” It's the only way in. kubectl, dashboards, and even the other parts all go through it.
📒 etcd“The order book.” A database that stores your wishes (desired state) and what's going on right now.
🪑 Scheduler“The host who seats guests.” When a new pod has no machine yet, it picks the best node (one with enough free CPU and memory).
🔁 Controller manager“The manager who keeps checking.” It runs the loops: “wanted 3, have 2, so make one more.”
💪 Every worker node has
👷 kubelet“The station chef.” It makes sure the containers assigned to this node are running, and reports back.
🐳 container runtimeUsually containerd. It pulls images and starts containers when kubelet asks.
🔀 kube-proxySets up networking so traffic reaches the right pod (more on that in the Services lesson).

Follow one request through the cluster

  1. You run kubectl apply. It goes to the API server.
  2. The API server saves your wish in etcd.
  3. A controller sees that a pod is needed and creates a pod record.
  4. The scheduler sees a pod with no node and assigns it to node-2.
  5. The kubelet on node-2 sees the assignment and tells the runtime to pull the image and start it.
  6. kubelet reports “Running” back to the API server.

This is the main coordination pattern: components watch the API server and react. The kubelet also talks to its local container runtime to actually start containers.

Remember
  • Cluster = control plane (brain) + worker nodes (muscle).
  • Everything goes through the API server. etcd remembers. The scheduler places. Controllers fix. kubelet runs.

quiz.q: You run a kubectl command. Which component receives it?
quiz.why: The API server is the front door for everything.

quiz.q: Where is the desired state stored?
quiz.why: etcd is the cluster's memory. Lose it and the cluster forgets everything (that's why we back it up in Stage 5).

quiz.q: Which component runs on every worker node and actually gets containers running?
quiz.why: kubelet is the agent on each node.

pod.title: Pods, and reading YAML without fear
pod.description: Kubernetes needs to know about your container: its image, its ports, how much memory it needs, and sometimes a helper container that must live right next to…
pod.html:
The problem
Kubernetes needs to know about your container: its image, its ports, how much memory it needs, and sometimes a helper container that must live right next to it.
The big idea
Kubernetes doesn't run bare containers. It runs Pods: a thin wrapper around one container (sometimes a few that belong together) that share an IP address and storage. A Pod is the smallest thing Kubernetes manages.
Think of it like…
Peas in a pod 🫛. Usually just one pea.

Pods are cattle, not pets 🐄

Pods are disposable. When one dies, Kubernetes doesn't fix it. It creates a brand-new pod with a new name and a new IP. Never rely on one specific pod. The next lessons show how to live with that.

Every YAML file has the same 4 parts

apiVersion: v1          # which version of the API this follows
kind: Pod               # WHAT you're describing
metadata:               # name + labels (tags)
  name: pizza
  labels:
    app: pizza
spec:                   # the wish: what it should look like
  containers:
  - name: pizza
    image: nginx:1.27
    ports:
    - containerPort: 80

Indentation matters (use 2 spaces, never tabs). A - means “an item in a list”. That's really all YAML is.

kubectl apply -f pod.yaml     # send the wish to the cluster
kubectl get pods              # see what's running
kubectl delete pod pizza      # gone, and nothing brings it back (yet!)
Remember
  • Pod = a wrapper around (usually) one container. The smallest thing K8s runs.
  • Pods are disposable: a new pod means a new name and a new IP.
  • Most workload manifests have apiVersion, kind, metadata, and spec. Some objects use other fields, such as data in a ConfigMap.

quiz.q: You delete a Pod owned by a Deployment. What happens?
options: The same pod gets repaired in place
A new pod is created, with a new name and IP
quiz.why: The Deployment replaces a deleted Pod. A crashed container can also restart inside an existing Pod.

quiz.q: What are the 4 top-level parts of almost every manifest?
quiz.why: Learn these 4 and any YAML file becomes readable.

quiz.q: Usually, how many containers are in a Pod?
quiz.why: One container per pod is the normal case. Extra “sidecar” containers are for special jobs like log shipping.

deploy.title: Deployments: stop looking after pods
deploy.description: You created a Pod by hand, then deleted it. Nothing created a replacement. Its kubelet can restart a crashed container inside a surviving Pod, but a deleted…
deploy.html:
The problem
You created a Pod by hand, then deleted it. Nothing created a replacement. Its kubelet can restart a crashed container inside a surviving Pod, but a deleted Pod needs a controller to replace it.
The big idea
Create a Deployment instead: “keep N copies of this pod running, always.” It's the thermostat from the first lesson. You almost never create Pods yourself. You create Deployments, and they create the Pods.

Under the hood: a Deployment manages a ReplicaSet, which keeps N Pods alive. (That middle layer matters for updates later. For now you can ignore it.)

🎮 Try it

Below is a fake cluster with 3 nodes running a Deployment of 3 pizza pods. Click a pod to delete it 🔨, and use + / − to change the number of replicas. Watch the event log.

📄 deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: pizza
spec:
  replicas: 3              # the wish: 3 copies
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: pizza           # "the pods I own have this label"
  template:                # the pod recipe (same as the Pod lesson!)
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: pizza
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: pizza
        image: nginx:1.27
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl get pods -w                      # -w = keep watching live
kubectl delete pod <one-of-the-pods>     # a replacement gets a new name
kubectl scale deployment pizza --replicas=6
Remember
  • Don't create Pods. Create Deployments.
  • replicas = how many copies. K8s keeps that number true forever.
  • To really remove pods, scale down or delete the Deployment. Deleting a pod just gets it replaced.

quiz.q: You delete a pod that belongs to a Deployment with replicas: 3. What happens?
options: A new pod is created to get back to 3
quiz.why: You saw it happen in the game.

quiz.q: How do you get 10 copies?
options: Set replicas to 10 (or use kubectl scale)
quiz.why: One number.

quiz.q: What is the template in a Deployment?
options: The pod recipe used to create every copy
quiz.why: Every pod the Deployment creates is stamped from that template.

challenge.text: Delete 3 pods, then scale up to 6 Running replicas.

nodedies.title: When a whole machine dies
nodedies.description: 3am. A hardware failure takes out node-2, along with every pod on it. The controller sees “wanted 4, have 2” and the scheduler places replacement pods on…
nodedies.html:
The problem
3am. A hardware failure takes out node-2, along with every pod on it.
The big idea
The controller sees “wanted 4, have 2” and the scheduler places replacement pods on the nodes that are still alive. Your app shrinks for a moment, then heals, if other nodes have room. Keeping another ready replica on a different node can keep the app serving while replacements start.

🎮 Try it

Choose Turn off on one machine and watch replacement pods appear elsewhere. Then choose Repair. Notice that pods do not move back when the node returns, because Kubernetes doesn't rebalance on its own. Bonus: kill all three nodes.

In a real cluster, Kubernetes waits about 5 minutes before deciding a silent node is truly dead (it might just be a network hiccup). This practice speeds that delay up so you can see recovery happen.

Remember
  • Pods never move. They're replaced.
  • Run at least 2 replicas of anything important.
  • Leave spare room on your nodes, or replacement pods will have nowhere to go.

quiz.q: You run replicas: 1 and its node dies. What do users see?
options: Downtime until a new pod starts somewhere else
The pod moves to another node without stopping
quiz.why: Pods don't move while running. They're recreated. With 2+ replicas on different nodes, the others keep serving.

quiz.q: node-2 comes back. Do the pods move back to it?
options: No. New pods may land there, but running pods stay where they are
quiz.why: Kubernetes only places pods when they're created.

challenge.text: Kill a node, wait until all 4 pods are Running again, then repair the node.

service.title: Services: one address for many pods
service.description: Your frontend needs to call the pizza app. But pizza pods keep dying and coming back with new IPs. Which IP do you put in your config?! A Service gives a…
service.html:
The problem
Your frontend needs to call the pizza app. But pizza pods keep dying and coming back with new IPs. Which IP do you put in your config?!
The big idea
A Service gives a group of pods one stable name and IP, and spreads requests across whichever pods are healthy right now. Callers just use http://pizza.
Think of it like…
A restaurant's phone number ☎️. Staff come and go, but customers always dial the same number, and whoever is on shift picks up.

How does it find the pods? Labels!

Pods carry name tags (labels) like app: pizza. The Service has a selector, app: pizza, meaning “send traffic to any pod with this tag”. Kubernetes updates EndpointSlices, the list of addresses behind the Service, as matching Pods become ready or disappear.

🎮 Try it

Send requests and watch how they're shared out. Then choose Start automatic requests and delete pods while it's running. Does any request fail?

📄 service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: pizza          # becomes the DNS name: http://pizza
spec:
  selector:
    app: pizza         # send to pods with this label
  ports:
  - port: 80           # the port callers use
    targetPort: 80     # the port the container listens on

The cluster has built-in DNS. Any pod can reach this Service at http://pizza (same namespace) or http://pizza.default.svc.cluster.local (from anywhere in the cluster).

kubectl expose deployment pizza --port=80   # creates the Service for you
kubectl get svc
kubectl get endpointslices                  # the live list of pod IPs behind it
Remember
  • Pods change. Services don't.
  • Service selector ↔ pod labels: that's what connects things in Kubernetes.
  • Inside the cluster, call services by name: http://pizza.

quiz.q: How does a Service decide which pods get traffic?
options: You list pod IPs in it
It picks random pods in the cluster
quiz.why: Labels + selectors.

quiz.q: Another pod wants to call our pizza Service. What address does it use?
quiz.why: DNS name = Service name.

quiz.q: A pod is deleted while traffic is flowing (3 replicas). What happens?
options: Requests go to the remaining pods
All requests fail until it's back
quiz.why: The Service removes shutting-down pods from its ready endpoints. Real connections and shutdown timing still need care; this model updates instantly.

challenge.text: Serve 40 requests while deleting at least 2 pods, with 0 failures.

outside.title: Letting the internet in
outside.description: The Service works inside the cluster. But your customers are on the internet. How do they get in? You choose how a Service is reachable with its type. For…
outside.html:
The problem
The Service works inside the cluster. But your customers are on the internet. How do they get in?
The big idea
You choose how a Service is reachable with its type. For websites, put one smart front door in front of all your Services: an Ingress, or its newer replacement, the Gateway API.
OptionWhat it doesUse it for
kubectl port-forwardtunnels a port to your laptopdebugging, local dev
ClusterIP (default)only reachable from inside the clusterdatabases, internal APIs
NodePortopens a port (30000–32767) on every nodequick tests, home labs
LoadBalancerthe cloud gives you a public IPone service = one public IP
Ingress / Gatewayone entry point that routes by hostname and pathwebsites with many services
Think of it like…
An Ingress is a building's reception desk 🛎️. One street address: “pizza.com/api, go to the API team; pizza.com, go to the web team.”
🌍 internet→🛎️ Ingress (pizza.com)→/api → Service api → pods/ → Service web → pods
⚠️ Common mistake: an Ingress is only a set of rules. Something has to carry them out: an ingress controller running as pods in the cluster (for example Traefik, which our k3s setup installs). With no controller, the rules do nothing.
📄 ingress.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: pizza
spec:
  rules:
  - host: pizza.local
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: pizza
            port:
              number: 80
kubectl port-forward svc/pizza 8080:80    # then open http://localhost:8080
Remember
  • ClusterIP = inside only (the default). LoadBalancer = public IP. Ingress = one smart front door.
  • Ingress rules need an ingress controller to do anything.

quiz.q: You want to quickly look at a service from your laptop while developing.
quiz.why: It's temporary and needs no setup.

quiz.q: Your database should NEVER be reachable from the internet. Which type?
quiz.why: ClusterIP is internal only, and it's the default.

quiz.q: You have 5 web apps and want them all on one public address, routed by hostname or path.
quiz.why: One front door, many rooms.

quiz.q: You created an Ingress but nothing works. What's the most likely cause?
quiz.why: It happens to everyone once.

config.title: Config & Secrets
config.description: Your pizza app needs a database address and a password. If you put them inside the image, you have to rebuild it for every environment, and anyone who pulls…
config.html:
The problem
Your pizza app needs a database address and a password. If you put them inside the image, you have to rebuild it for every environment, and anyone who pulls the image can read the password. 😬
The big idea
Keep config outside the image. A ConfigMap holds normal settings. A Secret holds sensitive values (passwords, tokens). Pods read them as environment variables or files.
Think of it like…
The same lunchbox (image) goes everywhere, but each office gets a different sticky note (config).
📄 configmap + secret + how a Deployment uses them
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: pizza-config
data:
  MENU_SIZE: "large"
  DB_HOST: "postgres"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: pizza-secret
stringData:              # write plain text; K8s stores it base64-encoded
  DB_PASSWORD: "s3cret!"
---
# inside the Deployment's container:
        envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: pizza-config
        - secretRef:
            name: pizza-secret
⚠️ Secrets are base64-encoded, not encrypted. Anyone who can read Secrets in the cluster can read your password. Limit who can read them (see the Security lesson), and never commit them to git as plain text. Tools like Sealed Secrets or External Secrets help later.

Gotcha: changing a ConfigMap does not restart pods. Environment variables are only read when a container starts, so restart the pods:

kubectl create configmap pizza-config --from-literal=MENU_SIZE=large
kubectl create secret generic pizza-secret --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD='s3cret!'
kubectl rollout restart deployment pizza     # pick up new config
Remember
  • Same image everywhere. Config comes from ConfigMaps and Secrets.
  • A Secret is not encrypted. Control who can read it.

quiz.q: Where should a database password go?
quiz.why: And then control who is allowed to read Secrets.

quiz.q: Is a Kubernetes Secret encrypted by default?
options: No, it's base64, which anyone can decode
quiz.why: echo czNjcmV0IQ== | base64 -d gives back s3cret!.

quiz.q: You changed a ConfigMap that's used as env vars, but the pods still see the old value. Why?
options: Env vars are read when the container starts, so restart the pods
quiz.why: kubectl rollout restart fixes it.

storage.title: Storage that survives
storage.description: You run a database in a pod. It restarts… and every order is gone. A container's filesystem is temporary: it's thrown away with the container. For data that…
storage.html:
The problem
You run a database in a pod. It restarts… and every order is gone. A container's filesystem is temporary: it's thrown away with the container.
The big idea
For data that must survive, ask for a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC): “I need 5 GB of disk.” With a suitable storage provider configured, the cluster finds or creates storage (a PersistentVolume) and attaches it to your pod. If the pod dies, the disk stays, and the new pod gets the same disk.
Think of it like…
A hotel 🏨. Pods are guests who check in and out. A PVC is a locker reservation: whoever holds it gets the same locker, with your things still inside.
TermWhat it isWho makes it
PVCthe request: “I need 5Gi”you
PVthe actual diskusually created automatically
StorageClassthe kind of disk, and who provides it (cloud SSD, local disk…)the cluster admin (k3s ships one called local-path)
📄 pvc.yaml + attaching it in a pod
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: pizza-data
spec:
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]   # one node at a time
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 5Gi
---
# in the pod spec:
      containers:
      - name: db
        image: postgres:17
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
      volumes:
      - name: data
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: pizza-data

A volume is not a backup. The local-path storage in our home lab lives on one machine. If that machine is lost, the data does not magically move to another one. Use suitable shared or replicated storage and separate backups when you need that protection.

Other kinds of workloads

KindUse it when
Deploymentstateless apps: web servers, APIs (most things)
StatefulSetdatabases: each replica gets a stable name (db-0, db-1) and its own disk
DaemonSetexactly one pod on every node: log collectors, monitoring agents
Job / CronJobrun something until it finishes, once or on a schedule (backups, reports)

Honest advice: for important production data, a managed database outside the cluster is often the calmer choice while you're learning.

Remember
  • A container's filesystem is temporary. Use a PVC for anything you want to keep.
  • Deployment for stateless apps, StatefulSet for databases, DaemonSet for one-per-node, CronJob for scheduled tasks.

quiz.q: A pod with no volume writes a file, then restarts. Is the file still there?
quiz.why: That's why PVCs exist.

quiz.q: What do you write to ask for storage?
quiz.why: A claim is a request. The cluster fulfils it.

quiz.q: You need one log-collector pod on EVERY node.
quiz.why: DaemonSet = one per node, automatically, including nodes added later.

quiz.q: A backup script that runs every night?
quiz.why: Like cron on Linux, but in the cluster.

health.title: Health checks & resource limits
health.description: Two sneaky problems: (1) your app is “running” but frozen, and Kubernetes keeps sending it traffic. (2) One pod leaks memory and eats the whole node,…
health.html:
The problem
Two sneaky problems: (1) your app is “running” but frozen, and Kubernetes keeps sending it traffic. (2) One pod leaks memory and eats the whole node, starving the pods next to it.
The big idea
Probes tell Kubernetes how to check your app's health. Requests and limits tell it how much CPU and memory your app needs and how much it's allowed to use.
ProbeQuestion it asksIf it fails…
🟢 readiness“Can you take traffic right now?”removed from the Service (not restarted)
❤️ liveness“Are you alive at all?”the container is restarted
🐢 startup“Still booting, give me time”holds off the other two for slow-starting apps
SettingMeaning
requestsThe reservation. The scheduler only places a pod on a node that has this much free.
limitsThe ceiling. Go over the memory limit and the container is killed (OOMKilled). Go over the CPU limit and it's slowed down, not killed.

🎮 Try it

This cluster has small nodes. Based on their requests, each node fits only 3 pizza pods. Scale up and see what happens when no node has room.

In this practice, a waiting pod is what kubectl describe pod would explain: 0/2 nodes are available: 2 Insufficient cpu. To fix it, scale down or add capacity. Lower requests only if measurements show the app really needs fewer resources.

📄 resources + probes in a container
      containers:
      - name: pizza
        image: nginx:1.27
        resources:
          requests: { cpu: "250m", memory: "128Mi" }  # 250m = 1/4 of a CPU core
          limits:   { memory: "256Mi" }
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet: { path: /, port: 80 }
          periodSeconds: 5
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet: { path: /, port: 80 }
          initialDelaySeconds: 10
Remember
  • Readiness = traffic on/off. Liveness = restart.
  • Requests = what the scheduler reserves. Limits = the hard ceiling.
  • Always set requests. Always set a memory limit.

quiz.q: A readiness probe fails. What does Kubernetes do?
options: Stops sending it traffic until the probe passes again
quiz.why: Readiness only controls traffic.

quiz.q: A liveness probe keeps failing. What happens?
quiz.why: That's what liveness is for: getting a stuck app unstuck.

quiz.q: A pod's status says OOMKilled. What does that mean?
options: It used more memory than its limit and was killed
quiz.why: OOM = Out Of Memory.

quiz.q: A pod is stuck Pending with “Insufficient cpu”. Why?
options: No node has enough unreserved CPU for its requests
quiz.why: You just made this happen in the game.

challenge.text: Create a waiting pod, then free enough room for every remaining copy.

rollout.title: Updates with no downtime (and undo!)
rollout.description: The old way to update: stop v1, start v2, and hope. Customers get errors in between, and if v2 is broken, everything is down. Change the image in your…
rollout.html:
The problem
The old way to update: stop v1, start v2, and hope. Customers get errors in between, and if v2 is broken, everything is down.
The big idea
Change the image in your Deployment and Kubernetes does a rolling update: start one new pod, wait until it's Ready, remove one old pod, repeat. This practice keeps all desired copies available and allows one extra copy. With readiness checks, spare capacity, and an app that shuts down cleanly, this can avoid downtime. If new pods never become Ready in this model, the rollout stalls while the old pods keep serving. Then you roll back with one command.

🎮 Try it

Choose Release a good version and wait for version 2. Requests start automatically. Next release a broken version, wait for a red pod, and choose Undo release.

kubectl set image deployment/pizza pizza=pizza:v2   # ship it
kubectl rollout status deployment/pizza              # watch it roll
kubectl rollout history deployment/pizza
kubectl rollout undo deployment/pizza                # go back to the previous version

The readiness probe from the last lesson is what makes this safe. Without one, Kubernetes thinks a pod is ready the moment it starts.

Other strategies exist: Recreate (stop everything, then start, for apps that can't run two versions at once), blue/green (switch all traffic at once) and canary (send 5% to the new version first). The rolling update is the default and usually enough.

Remember
  • Changing the image triggers a rolling update: new up, old down, one at a time.
  • A broken release stalls instead of taking you down.
  • kubectl rollout undo is your undo button.

quiz.q: During a rolling update, the new pods crash. What happens to the old ones?
options: They were already deleted, so you're down
They keep running and serving; the rollout stalls
quiz.why: In this practice, maxUnavailable is 0 and maxSurge is 1, so old copies stay available until their replacements are ready. Other rollout settings behave differently.

quiz.q: Which command goes back to the previous version?
quiz.why: Kubernetes keeps old ReplicaSets around for exactly this.

quiz.q: What makes K8s wait until a new pod is truly ready before removing an old one?
quiz.why: Without a readiness probe, a running container is usually treated as ready even if the app still needs time to prepare.

challenge.text: Ship a good release AND recover from a broken one with rollback, with 0 failed requests.

debug.title: Detective mode: debugging
debug.description: Something's broken. Don't panic. Almost every Kubernetes problem is solved with the same 4 commands, in this order. get → describe → logs → exec. Check the…
debug.html:
The problem
Something's broken. Don't panic. Almost every Kubernetes problem is solved with the same 4 commands, in this order.
The big idea
get → describe → logs → exec. Check the status, read the events, read the app's output, look around inside.
kubectl get pods                       # 1. what's the STATUS?
kubectl describe pod <name>            # 2. scroll to "Events" at the bottom. The answer is usually there
kubectl logs <name> --previous         # 3. what did the app say before it crashed?
kubectl exec -it <name> -- sh          # 4. open a shell inside the container
kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp   # bonus: what happened recently?

Status cheat sheet

You seeIt meansLook at
Pendingnot placed on a node yet: no room, or its disk (PVC) isn't readydescribe → Events
ContainerCreatingpulling the image or attaching volumeswait; describe if it's stuck
ImagePullBackOffwrong image name or tag, or a private image without credentialsdescribe
CrashLoopBackOffthe app starts, then exits, over and overlogs --previous
OOMKilledwent over its memory limitraise the limit, or fix the leak
CreateContainerConfigErrora ConfigMap or Secret it needs is missingdescribe
Running but 0/1 READYthe readiness probe is failing, so it gets no trafficdescribe + logs

Now the detective game. 🕵️ Solve these cases:

Remember
  • get → describe → logs → exec.
  • Pending = waiting to be scheduled or set up (use describe). CrashLoop = an app problem (use logs --previous).

quiz.q:
NAME        READY  STATUS            RESTARTS
pizza-7d9   0/1    ImagePullBackOff  0
Most likely cause?
options: A typo in the image name or tag (or a private image without credentials)
The node is out of memory
quiz.why: The container never started, so it can't be an app bug yet.

quiz.q:
NAME        READY  STATUS            RESTARTS
pizza-5c1   0/1    CrashLoopBackOff  5
What's the first command to run?
quiz.why: --previous shows the output of the container that just crashed.

quiz.q:
NAME        READY  STATUS   AGE
pizza-x2k   0/1    Pending  10m
Where will you find the answer?
options: It'll fix itself in an hour
quiz.why: Start with Events to learn whether scheduling, image downloads, or storage setup is blocking it. A container that has not started cannot produce app logs.

quiz.q:
NAME        READY  STATUS   RESTARTS
pizza-a1b   0/1    Running  0
It's running but gets no traffic. Why?
quiz.why: Running + 0/1 READY points to readiness.

security.title: Namespaces, permissions & staying safe
security.description: Your team grows. Dev and prod share one cluster, an intern has kubectl, and one pod gets hacked. Who can touch what? Namespaces are folders that keep things…
security.html:
The problem
Your team grows. Dev and prod share one cluster, an intern has kubectl, and one pod gets hacked. Who can touch what?
The big idea
Namespaces are folders that keep things apart. RBAC (role-based access control) decides who, people and pods alike, may do what. Kubernetes is not locked down by default, so you add a few basics.

Namespaces

kubectl create namespace prod
kubectl get pods -n prod      # look inside one namespace
kubectl get pods -A           # all namespaces

Names only have to be unique within a namespace. Reach a Service in another namespace with http://pizza.prod.

RBAC in one picture

📜 Role: “can get, list pods”+🔗 RoleBinding: “…given to alice”=✅ alice can read pods in prod

Nothing is allowed unless a binding allows it. Pods get an identity too, called a ServiceAccount, which you can grant permissions to the same way.

📄 role.yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  namespace: prod
  name: pod-reader
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods", "pods/log"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  namespace: prod
  name: alice-reads-pods
subjects:
- kind: User
  name: alice
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: pod-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n prod --as alice    # → no

The 5 security basics

  1. Don't give everyone cluster-admin. Grant the smallest permissions that work.
  2. Don't run containers as root (securityContext: runAsNonRoot: true).
  3. Set requests and limits so one runaway pod can't starve the rest.
  4. By default every pod can talk to every pod, across namespaces too. Use NetworkPolicies to restrict that.
  5. Keep Secrets out of git, and keep the cluster and your images updated.
Remember
  • Namespace = folder. Role = what's allowed. RoleBinding = who gets it.
  • Kubernetes is open by default. Lock it down on purpose.

quiz.q: How do you see pods in ALL namespaces?
quiz.why: -A = --all-namespaces.

quiz.q: By default, can a pod in namespace “dev” talk to a pod in “prod”?
options: Yes. You need NetworkPolicies to block it
quiz.why: Namespaces organize things. They don't isolate the network.

quiz.q: Role vs RoleBinding?
options: Role = a list of permissions; RoleBinding = who gets them
RoleBinding defines permissions; Role picks users
quiz.why: What is allowed, plus who it's given to.

helm.title: Helm: stop copy-pasting YAML
helm.description: Your app now has a Deployment, Service, Ingress, ConfigMap, Secret and PVC, for dev, staging and prod. You're copy-pasting YAML and changing 3 values each…
helm.html:
The problem
Your app now has a Deployment, Service, Ingress, ConfigMap, Secret and PVC, for dev, staging and prod. You're copy-pasting YAML and changing 3 values each time. 😩
The big idea
Helm is a package manager for Kubernetes, like brew or apt. A chart is a template for all those YAML files, and you fill in values (image tag, replicas, hostname) for each environment. One command installs, upgrades or rolls back the whole bundle.
helm repo add podinfo https://stefanprodan.github.io/podinfo
helm install my-app podinfo/podinfo --set replicaCount=3
helm upgrade my-app podinfo/podinfo --set replicaCount=5
helm list
helm rollback my-app 1
helm uninstall my-app
📄 One chart, different values per environment
# values-prod.yaml
replicaCount: 5
image:
  tag: v2
ingress:
  host: pizza.com

# then:
# helm install pizza ./pizza-chart -f values-prod.yaml

Also worth knowing: Kustomize is built into kubectl (kubectl apply -k) and patches plain YAML without templates. GitOps tools (Argo CD, Flux) make a git repo the source of truth, and a controller in the cluster keeps the cluster matching it. That's the reconciliation loop again!

Remember
  • Chart = templated YAML bundle. Values = your settings for each environment.
  • helm install / upgrade / rollback / uninstall.

quiz.q: A Helm chart is…
options: A bundle of templated K8s manifests with values you fill in
quiz.why: Think “app package”.

quiz.q: You want the same app in dev (1 replica) and prod (5 replicas).
options: Copy all the YAML into two folders and edit by hand
Two clusters with different kubectl versions
quiz.why: Same template, different values.

laptop.title: Your first real cluster (on your laptop)
laptop.description: Time to use a real cluster. Tick each box as you go; your progress is saved. You'll need Docker Desktop (or OrbStack or Colima) running. Install kubectl,…
laptop.html:
Time to use a real cluster. Tick each box as you go; your progress is saved. You'll need Docker Desktop (or OrbStack or Colima) running.

1 · Install the tools

brew install kubectl kind helm

2 · Create a 3-node cluster

kind = “Kubernetes IN Docker”. Each “node” is a container on your laptop, so it's fast and free to throw away.

cat > kind.yaml <<'EOF'
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
nodes:
- role: control-plane
- role: worker
- role: worker
EOF
kind create cluster --name pizza --config kind.yaml
kubectl config current-context   # should say kind-pizza
kubectl get nodes

Check that the context is kind-pizza before the exercises. A context tells kubectl which cluster it will change.

3 · Deploy and expose 🍕

kubectl create deployment pizza --image=nginx:1.27 --replicas=3
kubectl get pods -o wide
kubectl expose deployment pizza --port=80
kubectl port-forward svc/pizza 8080:80

This command stays running. Keep this terminal open while browsing; use a second terminal for the next exercises. Press Ctrl+C to stop forwarding. You will see the nginx welcome page: it stands in for our pizza app.

4 · Break it on purpose 🔨

kubectl delete pod -l app=pizza
kubectl get pods -w
docker stop pizza-worker
kubectl get nodes -w       # Ctrl+C stops watching; the cluster keeps running
docker start pizza-worker

5 · Update, break, roll back 🚀

kubectl set image deployment/pizza nginx=nginx:1.28
kubectl rollout status deployment/pizza
kubectl set image deployment/pizza nginx=nginx:does-not-exist
kubectl get pods          # ImagePullBackOff, but the old pods are still Running!
kubectl describe pod <the-broken-one>
kubectl rollout undo deployment/pizza

6 · The best trick: let kubectl write the YAML for you

kubectl create deployment pizza --image=nginx:1.27 --dry-run=client -o yaml > pizza.yaml
kubectl apply -f pizza.yaml

7 · Clean up

kind delete cluster --name pizza
🎉 If you ticked everything, you've done what a junior platform engineer does in their first week.

k3s.title: A real multi-machine cluster (k3s)
k3s.description: kind runs real Kubernetes nodes inside containers. Now let's use real (virtual) machines and k3s, a lightweight but fully certified Kubernetes that's great…
k3s.html:
kind runs real Kubernetes nodes inside containers. Now let's use real (virtual) machines and k3s, a lightweight but fully certified Kubernetes that's great for home labs, edge devices and learning.

k3s comes with the essentials built in: the Traefik ingress controller, a LoadBalancer implementation, local-path storage and metrics-server. We'll use Multipass to create 3 Ubuntu VMs on your Mac.

💡 Run every step in the same terminal window, because later steps reuse the $CP_IP and $TOKEN variables.

1 · Three machines

brew install --cask multipass
multipass launch --name cp --cpus 2 --memory 2G --disk 10G
multipass launch --name w1 --cpus 2 --memory 2G --disk 10G
multipass launch --name w2 --cpus 2 --memory 2G --disk 10G

2 · Install the control plane

multipass exec cp -- bash -c "curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io | sh -"
CP_IP=$(multipass info cp | awk '/IPv4/ {print $2}')
TOKEN=$(multipass exec cp -- sudo cat /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/node-token)
echo $CP_IP

3 · Join the workers

for w in w1 w2; do
  multipass exec $w -- bash -c "curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io | K3S_URL=https://$CP_IP:6443 K3S_TOKEN=$TOKEN sh -"
done

4 · Control it from your Mac

mkdir -p ~/.kube
multipass exec cp -- sudo cat /etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml | sed "s/127.0.0.1/$CP_IP/" > ~/.kube/k3s.yaml
export KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/k3s.yaml
kubectl get nodes          # cp, w1, w2: all Ready 🎉

A kubeconfig file tells kubectl which cluster to talk to and who you are. If you have several clusters, switch between them with kubectl config get-contexts / kubectl config use-context <name>.

5 · Deploy with a real Ingress

kubectl create deployment pizza --image=nginx:1.27 --replicas=3
kubectl expose deployment pizza --port=80
kubectl create ingress pizza --rule="pizza.local/*=pizza:80"
echo "$CP_IP pizza.local" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts
kubectl get pods -o wide
multipass stop w1
kubectl get nodes -w       # press Ctrl+C before the next command
multipass start w1

Where to go from here

  • Highly available control plane: 3 server nodes with embedded etcd (--cluster-init in k3s), so losing one doesn't take down the brain.
  • kubeadm: the official, more manual way to build a cluster. Do it once to see every moving part.
  • Managed Kubernetes (EKS, GKE, AKS): for serious production, the cloud runs the control plane for you.
multipass delete --purge cp w1 w2

day2.title: Day 2: keeping your cluster healthy
day2.description: Building a cluster is day 1. Keeping it healthy for months is day 2, and that's the real job. Here's what to set up and the routine to follow. Check CPU and…
day2.html:
Building a cluster is day 1. Keeping it healthy for months is day 2, and that's the real job. Here's what to set up and the routine to follow.

👀 1 · See what's happening

kubectl top nodes
kubectl top pods -A
brew install k9s && k9s
helm repo add prometheus-community https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts
helm install mon prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack -n monitoring --create-namespace
kubectl -n monitoring get secret mon-grafana -o jsonpath='{.data.admin-password}' | base64 -d; echo
kubectl -n monitoring port-forward svc/mon-grafana 3000:80    # log in as admin at http://localhost:3000

For logs from every pod in one place, add Grafana Loki later. In a home lab, kubectl logs and k9s are often enough.

💾 2 · Backups (a backup you've never restored is just a hope)

WhatHow
Cluster state (etcd)The single-server k3s setup here uses SQLite. Follow the K3s backup and restore instructions: preserve the database directory and /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/token, store a copy off the node, and test restoring it. With embedded etcd: sudo k3s etcd-snapshot save. With kubeadm: etcdctl snapshot save.
Your manifestsKeep all YAML and Helm values in git. Then the cluster itself can be rebuilt from scratch.
App data (PVCs)Use database-aware backups for databases. Tools such as Velero can back up resources and supported volumes when their storage integration is configured. Test a restore; a PVC by itself is not a backup.

⬆️ 3 · Upgrades

Kubernetes ships a new minor version about 3 times a year, and each one is supported for roughly a year. So plan an upgrade every few months.

  • Go one minor version at a time (1.33 → 1.34, never skip one).
  • Control plane first, then workers.
  • Read the release notes for removed APIs before you upgrade.
kubectl drain w1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data   # move pods off w1
# upgrade w1 (k3s: re-run the install script with INSTALL_K3S_VERSION=<next version>)
kubectl uncordon w1                                              # allow pods back

Add a PodDisruptionBudget to important apps so a drain never takes all their replicas down at once.

🔐 4 · Certificates & security

  • cert-manager + Let's Encrypt gives your websites HTTPS certificates that renew themselves.
  • The cluster's internal certificates usually last 1 year. Regular upgrades renew them (with kubeadm, check with kubeadm certs check-expiration).
  • Keep the node operating systems and your container images patched.
helm repo add jetstack https://charts.jetstack.io
helm install cert-manager jetstack/cert-manager -n cert-manager --create-namespace --set crds.enabled=true

🗓️ 5 · Your routine

WhenDo this
DailyGlance at the dashboards and alerts.
Weeklykubectl get pods -A | grep -vE 'Running|Completed' and kubectl get events -A --field-selector type=Warning
MonthlyPatch node OS and images. Test a restore. Check disk space on nodes.
QuarterlyUpgrade Kubernetes by one minor version.

grad.title: Graduation
grad.description: This is your finish line, not an automatic certificate. Try the tasks below without following the earlier commands line by line. Go back to a lesson…
grad.html:
This is your finish line, not an automatic certificate. Try the tasks below without following the earlier commands line by line. Go back to a lesson whenever you need it.

Your final mission

Use a disposable learning cluster and a small app. Check an item only after you have done it. Your first goal is confidence running a home lab; operating important production systems takes more practice and testing.

Done? You have reached the end of the core path. Keep one small project running and practice the Day 2 routine. Learn the optional topics below as that project needs them.

The whole picture on one page

ThingIn one line
Clustercontrol plane (brain) + worker nodes (muscle)
Podwrapper around a container; disposable
Deployment“keep N copies of this pod running”, plus rolling updates
Servicea stable name/IP that sends traffic to pods matching a label
Ingress / Gatewayone front door for HTTP, routes by hostname and path
ConfigMap / Secretsettings and passwords kept outside the image
PVC“I need a disk that survives”
Probesreadiness = traffic on/off, liveness = restart
Requests / limitsreservation / ceiling for CPU and memory
Namespace / RBACfolders / who may do what
Helmpackaged, templated YAML

kubectl in 10 commands

kubectl get pods -A                         # what's running everywhere
kubectl apply -f file.yaml                  # make the cluster match this file
kubectl describe pod <name>                 # details + Events (the debugging gold mine)
kubectl logs <name> [--previous] [-f]       # app output
kubectl exec -it <name> -- sh               # shell inside
kubectl scale deploy <name> --replicas=5
kubectl set image deploy/<name> <ctr>=<image>
kubectl rollout undo deploy/<name>
kubectl port-forward svc/<name> 8080:80
kubectl create ... --dry-run=client -o yaml # let kubectl write YAML for you
Optional next steps, after the final mission
  • Practise for free in your browser: killercoda.com has hundreds of Kubernetes scenarios.
  • Build your own app (any small API + database) and deploy it to your k3s cluster with a Helm chart. This is where it all sinks in.
  • Level up: autoscaling (HPA), the Gateway API, GitOps with Argo CD, Operators and CRDs.
  • The hard way: “Kubernetes The Hard Way” by Kelsey Hightower builds a cluster by hand, piece by piece.
  • Official references: Pod lifecycle, Deployments and rollout settings, and K3s backup and restore.
  • Get certified: CKAD (for app developers) → CKA (for cluster admins).
  • Deep-dive simulator: the will make a lot more sense now. Try its Playground tab.
